section.title: The Helper of Israel
section.sectionRationale: Continuing the Book of Comfort opened in chapter 40, this chapter puts the LORD on trial against every rival god, summoning the nations to a courtroom where He alone can declare the end from the beginning. In the middle of that courtroom scene He turns tenderly to Israel, His chosen servant, promising to help, strengthen, and redeem a people too weak and few to help themselves.
section.thesis: The LORD who alone raises up and casts down kings, who alone declared the future before it happened, is the same God who takes Israel's trembling, worm-like weakness by the hand and promises, again and again, do not fear, I will help you.
section.frameNote: Seven movements: the courtroom summons and the LORD's control of history; the panicked nations manufacturing idols for comfort; the LORD's tender word to His servant Israel, chosen and not rejected; the promise to the worm of Jacob that its Redeemer will help; water for the desert as a sign of God's care; the LORD's challenge to the idols to declare anything at all; and the closing verdict that the idols are nothing but wind.

units.label: Who has raised up one from the east

verses.text: “Be silent before Me, O islands, and let the peoples renew their strength. Let them come forward and testify; let us together draw near for judgment.

Who has aroused one from the east and called him to his feet in righteousness? He hands nations over to him and subdues kings before him. He turns them to dust with his sword, to windblown chaff with his bow.
He pursues them, going on safely, hardly touching the path with his feet.
Who has performed this and carried it out, calling forth the generations from the beginning? I, the LORD, the first and the last, I am He.”

units.label: The panicked nations and their idols

verses.text: The islands see and fear; the ends of the earth tremble. They approach and come forward.
Each one helps the other and says to his brother, “Be strong!”
The craftsman encourages the goldsmith, and he who wields the hammer cheers him who strikes the anvil, saying of the welding, “It is good.” He nails it down so it will not be toppled.

units.label: Do not fear, I am your God

verses.text: “But you, O Israel, My servant, Jacob, whom I have chosen, descendant of Abraham My friend,
I brought you from the ends of the earth and called you from its farthest corners. I said, ‘You are My servant.’ I have chosen and not rejected you.
Do not fear, for I am with you; do not be afraid, for I am your God. I will strengthen you; I will surely help you; I will uphold you with My right hand of righteousness.
Behold, all who rage against you will be ashamed and disgraced; those who contend with you will be reduced to nothing and will perish.
You will seek them but will not find them. Those who wage war against you will come to nothing.
For I am the LORD your God, who takes hold of your right hand and tells you: Do not fear, I will help you.

units.label: Fear not, O worm of Jacob
units.note: your Redeemer is the Holy One

verses.text: Do not fear, O {{tola|worm}} of Jacob, O few men of Israel. I will help you,” declares the LORD. “Your {{goel|Redeemer}} is the Holy One of Israel.
Behold, I will make you into a threshing sledge, new and sharp, with many teeth. You will thresh the mountains and crush them, and reduce the hills to chaff.
You will winnow them, and a wind will carry them away; a gale will scatter them. But you will rejoice in the LORD; you will glory in the Holy One of Israel.
The poor and needy seek water, but there is none; their tongues are parched with thirst. I, the LORD, will answer them; I, the God of Israel, will not forsake them.
I will open rivers on the barren heights, and fountains in the middle of the valleys. I will turn the desert into a pool of water, and the dry land into flowing springs.
I will plant cedars in the wilderness, acacias, myrtles, and olive trees. I will set cypresses in the desert, elms and boxwood together,
so that all may see and know, may consider and understand, that the hand of the LORD has done this and the Holy One of Israel has created it.”

units.label: Present your case
units.note: the LORD's challenge to the idols

verses.text: “Present your case,” says the LORD. “Submit your arguments,” says the King of Jacob.
“Let them come and tell us what will happen. Tell the former things, so that we may reflect on them and know the outcome. Or announce to us what is coming.
Tell us the things that are to come, so that we may know that you are gods. Yes, do something good or evil, that we may look on together in dismay.
Behold, you are nothing and your work is of no value. Anyone who chooses you is detestable.
I have raised up one from the north, and he has come, one from the east who calls on My name. He will march over rulers as if they were mortar, like a potter who treads the clay.
Who has declared this from the beginning, so that we may know, and from times past, so that we may say: ‘He was right’? No one announced it, no one foretold it, no one heard your words.
I was the first to tell Zion: ‘Look, here they are!’ And I gave to Jerusalem a herald of good news.
When I look, there is no one; there is no counselor among them; when I ask them, they have nothing to say.
See, they are all a delusion; their works amount to nothing; their images are as empty as the wind.

tola.gloss: Worm, a small, crushed, seemingly insignificant creature. Calling Israel a worm is deliberately humbling, a nation reduced by its own weakness and small numbers, yet it is precisely this worm that God promises to make into a threshing sledge able to crush mountains, entirely by His own strength working through their weakness.

goel.gloss: Redeemer, kinsman-redeemer, one who by right of family relationship pays a price to rescue a relative from debt, slavery, or danger, as Boaz redeems Ruth's family line. Naming the Holy One of Israel as Israel's go'el means their rescue is not distant charity but the act of one bound to them by covenant, a pattern Christ fulfills as the true kinsman-redeemer of His people.

basic.context: The LORD opens a courtroom, summoning the nations and their idols to answer a single question: who controls history, raising up and casting down kings? While the nations scramble to reassure themselves by building sturdier idols, the LORD turns with startling tenderness to Israel, His weak and fearful servant, promising again and again not to abandon them but to help, strengthen, and redeem them.
basic.hermeneutics: The 'one from the east' and 'one from the north' most likely anticipate Cyrus the Persian, later named explicitly in chapters 44 to 45, whose conquests the LORD claims to have foreseen and ordained long before they happened. The courtroom's real point is not merely predicting a Persian king but proving, against every rival god, that only the LORD can declare the future because only He governs it.
basic.originalLanguages: Israel is called the {{tola}}, worm, of Jacob, a picture of weakness and insignificance, yet this same worm is promised power to crush mountains because its {{goel}}, Redeemer, is the Holy One of Israel Himself, a kinsman-redeemer bound to rescue His own by covenant obligation and love, not distant obligation.
basic.typology: Israel's identity as the LORD's chosen servant, called from the ends of the earth and not rejected, verses 8 to 9, anticipates the true and faithful Servant of later chapters, who succeeds where Israel as a nation repeatedly failed. The go'el who redeems weak, worm-like Israel foreshadows Christ, the ultimate kinsman-redeemer who takes on our flesh in order to rescue us as family, not as a stranger.
basic.christ: The title go'el, Redeemer, applied here to the Holy One of Israel, is the same office the New Testament ascribes to Christ, who became our brother in the flesh precisely so He could redeem us as family, Hebrews 2:14-17, Galatians 4:4-5. The LORD's self-declaration, 'I, the LORD, the first and the last,' verse 4, is the very title the risen Christ applies to Himself in Revelation 1:17, showing His full identity with the God who speaks in this chapter.
basic.god: God alone controls the rise and fall of nations and kings, and He alone can genuinely declare what is coming before it happens, exposing every idol as empty wind by comparison. Yet this same sovereign God stoops to call Israel's weakness a worm with tenderness rather than contempt, promising personal strength, help, and redemption to those who cannot help themselves.
basic.crossReferences: Ruth 4:1-10 shows the kinsman-redeemer pattern in action, as Boaz redeems Ruth's family line. Revelation 1:17 has the risen Christ declare Himself 'the First and the Last,' echoing verse 4. Hebrews 2:14-17 explains why Christ shared our humanity, to become a merciful and faithful redeemer. Galatians 4:4-5 describes God sending His Son to redeem those under the law.
basic.oneStory: This chapter puts the LORD on trial against every false god and finds Him alone able to declare and direct history, then turns that same sovereign power into tender, personal help for weak, fearful Israel. It anticipates Christ, the true Redeemer who takes on flesh to rescue His people as family, fulfilling both the courtroom's verdict and the covenant's promise.

context.literary:
The chapter is a trial scene in the form of a Hebrew lawsuit, and the vocabulary, 'judgment' in verse 1 and 'present your case' in verse 21, belongs to the courtroom. What gives it shape is a symmetry that the seven movements of the basic outline can hide: the trial opens and closes on the same subject, and the section in the middle is about Israel.

The frame is the question of who raised up a conqueror from the east. It is asked in verses 2 to 4 and answered at last in verses 25 to 29, where the LORD says, 'I have raised up one from the north, and he has come.' Inside that frame the idols appear twice. In verses 5 to 7 the craftsmen cheer one another on, 'Be strong!', and nail the idol down so that it will not topple, and in verses 21 to 24 the idols themselves are summoned and found speechless. At the centre, between the two idol scenes, stands the long, warm address to Israel in verses 8 to 20, in which the LORD says 'do not fear' three times and 'I will help you' three times, in verses 10, 13 and 14.

The pattern, then, runs from the trial to the idol-makers to Israel and back to the idol-makers and the trial. The arrangement is a lesson in itself. Israel's comfort is placed in the middle of the controversy over the gods, protected on both sides by the LORD's superior knowledge of history.

There is also a shift of mood at verse 8. Everything before it is a summons and a challenge. 'But you, O Israel' turns the sentence from the language of a court to that of a family. The section of verses 17 to 20 carries the same movement into the wilderness: God answers the poor and needy with water, and the purpose is stated as testimony, 'so that all may see and know.' The chapter ends where the second trial ended, with idols that are 'a delusion' and 'as empty as the wind.'
context.historical:
The 'one from the east' stirs the reader to ask who, and the book will answer by name. In Isaiah 44:28 the LORD says of Cyrus, 'My shepherd will fulfill all that I desire,' and in Isaiah 45:1 He calls him 'His anointed.' Cyrus began as a ruler in Persia, the land east of Babylon, and in the span of a few years overran the Median kingdom and, to the west, the kingdom of Lydia in Asia Minor. That explains the nations in verses 1 and 5, the 'islands' or coastlands that watch him come, see and fear. In 539 BC Babylon fell to him, and in the first year of his rule he issued the proclamation that let exiles go up to Jerusalem, 2 Chronicles 36:22 and 23 and Ezra 1:1.

The chapter belongs, then, to a world in which the exiles in Babylon were watching an unfamiliar power rise in the east. For a people with little left, this could look like one more empire that would swallow them. Isaiah's hearers are told that the conqueror is raised up by the LORD and that his campaigns are tools in His hand. The notice that he goes on 'hardly touching the path with his feet,' verse 3, catches the speed of the conquests.

The condition of Israel in this chapter is stated in the language of poverty. They are 'few men,' a 'worm.' After 586 BC the nation had no king, no army and no land of its own. The 'poor and needy' of verse 17 can be read as the exiles themselves, and their thirst on the way home across the desert is both literal and symbolic. The text calls Abraham 'My friend' in verse 8, and Jehoshaphat's prayer in 2 Chronicles 20:7 had used the same title for Abraham, with the same hope of help in a day of national peril.

Finally, the idol-making of verses 5 to 7 and 21 to 29 is not a straw man. Ancient religion centred on images made by craftsmen, and the nations 'comfort' themselves with new ones as the fear grows. Isaiah is observing a real response to crisis: when a threat arrives, build a sturdier god.
context.canonical:
The title 'My servant' is introduced here and becomes central. Israel is called servant in verses 8 and 9 and again in Isaiah 44:1 and 2 and 49:3, 'You are My Servant, Israel, in whom I will display My glory.' But in Isaiah 42:1, 'Here is My Servant, whom I uphold, My Chosen One,' the Servant begins to look like a person with a mission to the nations and to Israel. The two figures run side by side through the book. The New Testament takes the second and applies it to Jesus, Matthew 12:17 to 21.

The address 'Do not fear, for I am with you' belongs to the patriarchs and the exodus. God says it to Abraham, 'Do not be afraid, Abram. I am your shield,' Genesis 15:1; to Isaac, Genesis 26:24; and to the people before Joshua, 'He will never leave you nor forsake you,' Deuteronomy 31:6. In the same book it will return in Isaiah 43:1 and 5 and 44:2. The New Testament reaches for it when it says, 'The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid,' Hebrews 13:6, quoting Psalm 118:6. It is among the oldest and most repeated comforts in Scripture.

The claim in verse 4, 'I, the LORD, the first and the last, I am He,' echoes through Isaiah in 44:6 and 48:12, and then through the New Testament, where the risen Christ says, 'I am the First and the Last, the Living One,' Revelation 1:17 and 18, and 'the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End,' Revelation 22:13. The 'I am' sayings of Jesus, such as 'before Abraham was born, I am!' John 8:58, are heard against this background, as is the divine name of Exodus 3:14.

The court scene is repeated in Isaiah 43:9 to 13, 44:6 to 8 and 45:20 to 21, with the test of prediction as its centre. Deuteronomy 18:21 and 22 had already made fulfilment the test of a true prophet. And the water in the desert, verses 17 to 20, returns in Isaiah 43:19 and 20 and 44:3, where the water becomes the Spirit poured out on Israel's descendants.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer wants two things at once, and the chapter's form shows that they depend on each other. He wants Israel to be certain that the LORD alone governs history, and he wants Israel to be certain that this same LORD is on their side. If the first were true without the second, the exiles would be right to fear. If the second were true without the first, their comfort would be wishful.

The proof he offers is a particular one: the LORD can say what will happen before it does. The test is specific and public. The idols are challenged to 'tell the former things' and 'announce what is coming,' and they are silent. For the first hearers this was not an abstract argument. It was an invitation to look at the world after the event and see whose word had been right.

The writer also means to change how Israel sees itself. They are 'few,' they feel like a worm, and nothing in their circumstances proves their worth. The chapter does not flatter. It does not tell them they are strong. It says that they are 'chosen and not rejected,' and that the strength is the LORD's. The repeated 'do not fear' is the heart of the matter, each time grounded in a reason that has to do with God and not with them: 'for I am with you,' 'for I am your God,' 'I will help you.'

Finally, he means for them to hear a call to testimony. The water, the trees and the courtroom all serve the same aim: that 'all may see and know, may consider and understand, that the hand of the LORD has done this.'
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a historical argument and a set of promises made to Israel at a particular crisis. The promise that Israel would thresh mountains and that its enemies would 'come to nothing' is not a template that every believer's circumstances will follow, nor is it a command to wage war. The language of the threshing sledge is the poetry of a covenant people who will see their oppressors fall, and Micah 4:13 uses it in a similar way.

What the passage prescribes is a posture rather than an event. It tells the people not to fear, which is as much an instruction as a comfort. It tells them to trust a God who has shown Himself able. It also shows, by example, how to answer idolatry: with the evidence of God's word fulfilled.

It is unwise to take the promises of verse 10 as a guarantee of ease. The same people who hear 'I will uphold you' are called a worm and still had a hard road. The help promised is the LORD's presence and strength, which is what the New Testament builds on when it says, 'Surely I am with you always,' Matthew 28:20, and 'My power is perfected in weakness,' 2 Corinthians 12:9.

Nor is the courtroom passage a mandate for believers to humiliate other religions. It records the LORD's challenge to idols, and it is spoken by Him. What carries forward is the example of Paul in Acts 17:29, who speaks to idolaters with the same insight, and does so with respect for the people who hold the idols.

debates.question: Who is the 'one from the east' in verse 2?

views.label: Cyrus of Persia
views.case: The book itself names Cyrus in Isaiah 44:28 and 45:1 to 4, and describes him as summoned by the LORD for His purpose, Isaiah 46:11, and Ezra 1:1 says the LORD 'stirred the spirit of Cyrus.' The verb for 'aroused' in verses 2 and 25 is the same one. Persia lay east of Babylon, and the conquests of verses 2 and 3 suit the speed of his rise. This is the dominant reading.

views.label: Abraham
views.case: A long Jewish tradition, including Rashi, reads verse 2 as Abraham. The phrase 'called him to his feet in righteousness' suits the one named 'My friend' in verse 8, and Genesis 14:14 to 16 shows Abram routing the kings who had taken Lot and pursuing them. Abraham also came from the east. The weakness of the reading is verse 25, which says that the LORD has raised him up and that he 'will march over rulers as if they were mortar,' which sounds like the ongoing career of a conqueror.

views.label: Deliberately unnamed
views.case: Isaiah withholds the name here and names Cyrus only in chapters 44 and 45. On this view the point of verses 2 to 4 is the LORD's authorship of the conqueror, and the unnamed figure lets the argument stand on the pattern of God's rule: whenever such a figure appears, it is He who raised him.

debates.bearing: The question affects detail more than doctrine. If it is Cyrus, the chapter is a prediction that is later vindicated. If it is Abraham, it is a memory of an earlier act of God. Either way, the argument of the verses is the same: the LORD directs the rise and fall of those who seem to rule.

debates.question: Who is the 'servant' of verse 8, and is the Servant of later chapters the same?

views.label: The Servant is always the nation
views.case: Isaiah 41:8, 44:1 and 49:3 each name the Servant as Israel. On this view the later passages describe the nation, or its faithful remnant, and the 'individual' language is a poetic personification.

views.label: The Servant begins as the nation and becomes one who represents it
views.case: Israel is called servant here, but fails in the book, Isaiah 42:19. The later songs describe a servant who suffers for Israel and gives light to the nations, Isaiah 42:6 and 7 and 49:5 and 6. The writer moves from the nation that fails to a person who does what the nation could not.

views.label: The language points straight to Christ
views.case: Matthew reads Isaiah 42:1 to 4 as Jesus, Matthew 12:17 to 21, and Philip takes Isaiah 53 to the Ethiopian as good news about Jesus, Acts 8:35. On this view the whole servant theme is fulfilled in the person of Christ, with the nation's calling as its background.

debates.bearing: In chapter 41 the Servant is plainly Israel, chosen and not rejected. The question of how that identity opens out is one that the later chapters take up, and the New Testament answers it by pointing to Jesus as the faithful Israelite in whom the calling is fulfilled. That is why Paul can say that those who belong to Christ are 'Abraham's seed,' Galatians 3:29.

debates.question: Do the promises of verses 10 to 16 belong directly to Christians?

views.label: They are for Israel only
views.case: The passage is addressed to 'Jacob' and 'Israel' and speaks of their enemies and their land. On this view, applying them straight to the church overlooks the covenant setting.

views.label: They belong to all God's people in Christ
views.case: Paul says that those who belong to Christ are Abraham's seed and heirs, Galatians 3:29, and the New Testament applies the 'do not fear' and 'I am with you' to the church, Hebrews 13:5 and 6, Luke 12:32. The promises belong to the people of God as a whole.

views.label: The character of God carries forward, the particulars do not
views.case: The unchanging element is the LORD's help, not the form it takes. Threshing mountains is the language of Israel's exile, but the God who says 'I will help you' has not changed.

debates.bearing: The third view makes a useful rule: take the promise of presence and strength as certain, and take the shape of its fulfilment from the way Scripture itself carries it forward. The second view is supported by the New Testament's own habit.

study.originalLanguages:
Several words in this chapter repay a slower reading.

The word 'help' in verses 10, 13 and 14 comes from the root azar, the same root as ezer, the word used of the woman as a 'helper' in Genesis 2:18. The word is not about inferiority: it is used of God again and again, 'He is our help and our shield,' Psalm 33:20, and 'My help comes from the LORD,' Psalm 121:2. To call God Israel's helper is to use a word that can mean one who comes alongside and acts with real power.

The verbs of verse 10 come in a cluster. 'I will strengthen you' uses amats, the verb of 'Be strong and courageous' in Joshua 1:9, and 'I will uphold you' uses tamak, to hold up, to grasp. In verse 13 God 'takes hold' of Israel's right hand. The verb is chazaq, to be or to make strong, to grip. The same word, as a command, is what the craftsmen say to each other in verse 6, 'Be strong!' Nations urge one another to be strong; the LORD actually takes hold of a hand and does the strengthening.

Verse 8 calls Abraham 'My friend.' The Hebrew is ohavi, 'the one who loves Me,' from the verb ahav, to love. It is a covenant word, and 2 Chronicles 20:7 uses it of Abraham with the pronoun 'Your friend.' James picks up the title, 'he was called a friend of God,' James 2:23. The relationship begins in love, and Israel is the child of that love.

Righteousness frames the chapter. In verse 2 the conqueror is called 'in righteousness,' in verse 10 God upholds with 'My right hand of righteousness,' and in verse 26 the people would say of the one who declared the future, 'He was right.' The Hebrew word tsedeq, with its related adjective tsaddiq, appears in all three, and it carries the idea of what is right and what is rightly done. The whole chapter moves from the LORD's rightness in history to His rightness toward His own.

In verses 2 and 25 the verb for 'aroused' is the one that means to wake or stir. It is the verb used when 'the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus,' Ezra 1:1. God is the one who wakes conquerors.

The ending uses two powerful words. The idols are 'wind and emptiness,' ruach and tohu, in verse 29. The first is the word for breath, wind and spirit, and the second is the 'formless' of Genesis 1:2. The gods of the nations are an empty chaos, set against the LORD, who in verse 20 'created' the new world of springs and trees. The verb is bara, the one reserved in Genesis 1 for God's own creating.

The call in verse 21, 'Present your case,' uses rib, the word for a legal dispute, and 'King of Jacob' sets God as both plaintiff and judge.

typology.type: Israel, the chosen servant, verses 8 and 9
typology.fulfillment: Israel is God's servant, chosen and not rejected, called from the ends of the earth. In the next chapter the voice says, 'Here is My Servant, whom I uphold, My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights,' Isaiah 42:1, and Matthew applies it to Jesus, Matthew 12:17 to 21. Matthew also says that when Jesus came out of Egypt, Hosea's 'Out of Egypt I called My Son' was fulfilled, Matthew 2:15. The correspondence is that Christ is the true Israel, the Servant who fulfils what the nation was called to be. The type falls short in that Israel's servanthood was marked by failure, while Christ's is faithful to the end.

typology.type: The hand that takes hold and helps, verses 10 to 14
typology.fulfillment: The LORD says, 'I take hold of your right hand and tell you: Do not fear, I will help you.' When Peter sank in the waves, 'Jesus reached out His hand and took hold of Peter,' Matthew 14:31. Hebrews puts the two halves together with unusual precision: 'it is not the angels He helps, but the descendants of Abraham,' Hebrews 2:16. The same three elements are in Isaiah 41, a hand, help, and the descendants of Abraham. The type falls short at the place Hebrews names next: 'He had to be made like His brothers in every way,' Hebrews 2:17, because the help comes through the Helper's sharing in our flesh and death.

typology.type: Water in the desert, verses 17 to 20
typology.fulfillment: The poor and needy find their tongues parched, and the LORD opens rivers on bare heights, makes the desert a pool and plants it with trees. Isaiah 44:3 explains the water as the Spirit: 'I will pour water on the thirsty land... I will pour out My Spirit on your descendants.' Jesus stands on the last day of the feast and cries, 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink,' John 7:37, and says of the water He gives that it becomes 'a fount of water springing up to eternal life,' John 4:14. The Bible ends with the same invitation, Revelation 22:17. The type falls short in that the desert pools of Isaiah are signs of restoration, while the water of Christ is the Spirit Himself.

typology.type: The conqueror raised from the east, verses 2 and 25
typology.fulfillment: Cyrus is given a title in Isaiah 45:1, 'His anointed,' and he sets exiles free and sends them home to rebuild the house of God. In Luke 4:18 and 19 Jesus reads of One anointed 'to proclaim liberty to the captives,' and says it is fulfilled in Him. The pattern is of a deliverer raised up by God for captives. But it is held lightly. Cyrus is a pagan who does not know the LORD, Isaiah 45:4, and the freedom he gives is political and temporary. Christ frees from the slavery of sin and death, Hebrews 2:15, and does it by His own sacrifice, not by conquest.

study.christ:
Isaiah 41 leads to Christ by an identity, a title and a task.

The identity is in verse 4. 'I, the LORD, the first and the last, I am He.' The prophet's God declares the end from the beginning and is Himself both limits of history. When the risen Christ appears to John, He says, 'I am the First and the Last, the Living One. I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever and ever!' Revelation 1:17 and 18, and again, 'the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End,' Revelation 22:13. These are not borrowed phrases. They are the same claim, made by the same speaker, and the New Testament means us to hear it that way. The words that make the idols look foolish in Isaiah are the words Christ uses of Himself.

The title is in verse 14, where Israel's Redeemer is 'the Holy One of Israel.' In Hebrews, the Son shares our flesh and blood in order to redeem, 'so that He might become a merciful and faithful high priest,' Hebrews 2:17, and Galatians says that 'God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law,' Galatians 4:4 and 5. The mark of the Redeemer in Israel's law was kinship, as with Boaz and Ruth, Ruth 3:9, and Leviticus 25:25 spoke of 'his nearest of kin.' The Redeemer must be family. The incarnation is how the Holy One of Israel becomes our kin.

The task is the help of verses 10, 13 and 14. Hebrews quotes a psalm to say, 'The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid,' Hebrews 13:6, and says of Jesus that 'it is not the angels He helps, but the descendants of Abraham,' Hebrews 2:16. The help is personal and it takes hold of the hand, as Jesus took hold of the sinking Peter in Matthew 14:31. And Paul draws the great conclusion in Romans 8:31, 'If God is for us, who can be against us?', continuing with the Christ who 'died, and more than that was raised to life, is at the right hand of God,' and 'is interceding for us,' Romans 8:34. Isaiah's 'those who rage against you will be ashamed' becomes 'Who is there to condemn us?'

There is a quieter link in verse 9, 'I have chosen and not rejected you.' Jesus says of those the Father gives Him, 'the one who comes to Me I will never drive away,' John 6:37. The unrejected servant of Isaiah is the pattern of those who are in Christ.

The Servant language of verse 8 also begins a road that leads to Christ. The next chapter's Servant is the One in whom God's soul delights, and Matthew says that Jesus fulfils that, Matthew 12:17 to 21.

Not every detail should be forced. Cyrus is not a code name for Jesus, and the threshing sledge is not a picture of the cross. The links hold where the New Testament makes them: the divine title, the Redeemer's kinship, and the helping hand.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who is both a judge and a friend, and it does not let either description cancel the other.

He is the Lord of history. Verses 2 to 4 ask who raised up the conqueror, called the generations from the beginning, and carried everything out, and the answer is God Himself. He is the 'first and the last,' before every empire and after it. Nations are not independent forces to be reckoned with. They are things He has summoned and set in order, and the rise of Persia in the east is as much His work as the rebuilding of the temple that Cyrus will permit.

He is the God who knows and declares. The test He sets the idols is a test of knowledge: 'Tell the former things, so that we may reflect on them and know the outcome.' To know the end from the beginning is the mark of One who governs. That is why verse 26 asks, 'Who has declared this from the beginning, so that we may know?' His word precedes events and the events then confirm His word.

He is the God who stoops. 'But you, O Israel, My servant' turns the whole tone of the chapter. The same One who holds the nations in His hand takes hold of the right hand of a small, frightened people. He calls Abraham 'My friend.' He says, 'I am your God,' as someone who belongs to them. He does not wait for them to prove themselves; He says He has 'chosen and not rejected' them, which is grace and not merit, as Moses had said it, 'The LORD did not set His affection on you and choose you because you were more numerous,' Deuteronomy 7:7.

He is the God who helps. The word help comes three times and it is given not by an assistant but by the LORD Himself. The fear of Israel is met with His presence. 'I am with you' stands behind the promise as its reason.

He is the God who creates and provides. He opens rivers on barren heights and plants cedars in the desert, and then says the purpose: 'so that all may see and know... that the hand of the LORD has done this and the Holy One of Israel has created it.' Provision is a witness to His character.

He is the God who will not share His glory with anything made. He reduces the idols to 'nothing' and 'wind.' That is not contempt for people but the refusal to let a lie take the place of the truth that saves them.

For worship, this means we may come to God in our smallness. We do not have to be strong, or to flatter ourselves, or to hide that we feel like a worm. The God who weighs nations is the God who holds our hand, and the right response to His 'do not fear' is to believe it and then to tell what He has done.

crossReferences.note: God's first 'Do not be afraid' to Abram: 'I am your shield, your very great reward.' Isaiah's 'do not fear' to Abraham's descendants takes the same words and the same ground, that God Himself is the protection. It shows that Isaiah 41 is the renewal of an old promise, not a new one.

Jehoshaphat prays in a national crisis and calls Abraham God's friend, asking Him to remember His people. Isaiah 41:8 uses the same title. It shows that the title was used in prayer before the exile and that Isaiah is calling on a known and loved description.

Moses says the LORD chose Israel not because they were numerous, 'for you were the fewest of all peoples,' but because He loved them. It sits beneath Isaiah's 'few men' and 'worm' and shows that Israel's weakness never was the obstacle to election.

The passage names the one from the east: 'This is what the LORD says to Cyrus His anointed.' It resolves the question verse 2 raises and adds that the LORD calls him 'though you have not known Me,' showing that the LORD's use of a ruler does not depend on the ruler's faith.

The fulfilment in history: 'the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia' to send a proclamation letting the exiles return. The Hebrew verb is the same as the 'aroused' of Isaiah 41:2 and 25. It is the narrative closing of the argument that Isaiah makes.

Another courtroom scene, in which Israel is the LORD's witness: 'Before Me no god was formed, and after Me none will come.' The idols are challenged again, and Israel is asked to testify. It shows where the argument of chapter 41 leads: the people who were comforted become the ones who bear witness.

The very next chapter takes the word 'servant' and gives it a face: 'Here is My Servant, whom I uphold, My Chosen One.' It echoes the 'uphold' of 41:10 and is the first step from the nation as servant to the Servant who will bring justice, and Matthew applies it to Jesus.

The New Testament explanation of how the Redeemer redeems: He shares flesh and blood, frees those enslaved by fear of death, and 'helps' Abraham's descendants. It reads Isaiah's 'descendant of Abraham' and 'I will help you' together, and it is the most exact use of the chapter in the New Testament.

The risen Christ places His right hand on the fallen John and says 'Do not be afraid,' then 'I am the First and the Last.' The two halves of Isaiah 41, the 'do not fear' and the 'first and the last,' are spoken together by Jesus.

Peter begins to sink and cries 'Lord, save me!' and Jesus 'reached out His hand and took hold of Peter.' It is a living version of 41:13, 'who takes hold of your right hand and tells you: Do not fear,' and shows the same God doing the same thing.

The writer gives the promise, 'Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you,' and then the believer's reply, 'The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid.' It shows how the church took Israel's promises and made them its own confession.

On the last day of the feast Jesus calls the thirsty to come to Him. It answers Isaiah's picture of the thirsty poor and the LORD who will not forsake them, and says that the water, in Isaiah 44:3 the Spirit, now flows from those who believe in Him.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a God who speaks creation into order, and then a fall in which humanity trusts something other than Him. Idolatry is that same move, repeated: taking something made and treating it as the source of help. Isaiah 41 puts the first sin on trial. The craftsman nails down his god so it will not topple, and the LORD calls the whole business 'wind and emptiness,' the chaos of Genesis 1:2 which creation was meant to leave behind.

The chapter then answers a question asked from the call of Abraham onward: will God keep His promise to a people who are small, sinful and far from home? Genesis 12 had promised blessing through Abraham, and this chapter calls his descendants God's chosen servants, and calls Abraham His friend. The exile looked like the end of the promise. Isaiah says it is not; the God who made it is the God who will carry it out.

It looks ahead in two directions. In history it points to Cyrus, whose decree sends the exiles home, Ezra 1:1, and to the second exodus the prophets describe, with water in the desert and a way through the wilderness. In redemption it points to a Redeemer who is the Holy One Himself and yet a kinsman, a Servant who will be everything Israel was called to be.

The Gospels announce that He has come. Jesus is the helping hand that takes hold of the sinking, the Redeemer who becomes family by taking flesh, the One who says 'Do not be afraid' and 'I am the First and the Last,' and the water for the thirsty. Through Him the promise to Abraham reaches the nations, and 'all the families of the earth' are blessed, Genesis 12:3, as Paul says the promises were confirmed 'so that the Gentiles may glorify God for His mercy,' Romans 15:8 and 9.

The story ends where Isaiah 41:17 to 19 points. The desert becomes a garden, the water never fails, and the tree of life bears fruit 'for the healing of the nations,' Revelation 22:2. The idols are gone, and the worm of Jacob and all the redeemed live under the One who 'will wipe away every tear,' Revelation 21:4. The word 'help' has become a gift that is complete. In that city the people no longer need to be told 'do not fear,' because they live in the presence of the God who said it.

sermon.title: Fear Not, I Am with You, I Am Your God
sermon.why: Piper walks through Isaiah 41:1-10, showing how the LORD's identity as judge of the nations, ruler of history, and covenant God grounds the five pillars of fearlessness given to Israel in this chapter, the same promise he says has relieved his own fears more than any other verse in Scripture.

quiz.q: What question does the LORD press upon the nations and their idols in the opening courtroom scene, verses 1 to 4?

options.text: Who has raised up and directed the conqueror shaping history, and who alone declared this from the beginning?
options.note: Verses 2 to 4 press exactly this question, answered by the LORD's self-declaration as the first and the last.

options.text: Which nation has the strongest army?
options.note: The question concerns who controls and foretells history, not merely military strength.

options.text: Which idol is the most beautifully crafted?
options.note: The chapter later mocks idol-making, but the opening courtroom question concerns control of history, not craftsmanship.

options.text: Which nation deserves to be punished first?
options.note: The immediate courtroom question is about sovereignty over history and prophecy, not a ranking of guilt.

quiz.q: How do the nations respond to the coming threat in verses 5 to 7?

options.text: In fear, they encourage each other and rush to strengthen their idols so they will not topple.
options.note: Verses 5 to 7 describe exactly this panicked mutual encouragement and idol-making.

options.text: They calmly turn to the LORD for help.
options.note: The opposite; they turn to strengthening their own idols rather than to the LORD.

options.text: They immediately surrender without any response.
options.note: The text describes active, anxious effort, encouraging one another and reinforcing idols, not passive surrender.

options.text: They form a military alliance to fight back.
options.note: The described response is craftsmen reinforcing idols, not a military mobilization.

quiz.q: What repeated promise does the LORD give to Israel in verses 8 to 13?

options.text: Do not fear, for I am with you; I will strengthen, help, and uphold you.
options.note: This promise is repeated multiple times across verses 8 to 13.

options.text: Israel has been rejected and must fend for itself.
options.note: The opposite; the LORD explicitly says, 'I have chosen and not rejected you.'

options.text: Israel must first prove its own strength before receiving help.
options.note: The promise of help is given unconditionally to weak, fearful Israel, not as a reward for proven strength.

options.text: Israel's enemies will be given permanent victory.
options.note: The opposite; those who contend with Israel are promised shame and disgrace, not victory.

quiz.q: What title is given to the LORD in verse 14 in connection with helping Israel?

options.text: Your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel.
options.note: Verse 14 gives this exact title, connecting redemption directly to Israel's help in weakness.

options.text: A distant judge with no personal connection to Israel.
options.note: The opposite; Redeemer implies a close, covenantal, kinship-based relationship, not distance.

options.text: A foreign king who conquers on Israel's behalf.
options.note: The title given is Redeemer and Holy One of Israel, describing the LORD Himself, not a foreign ruler.

options.text: An angel sent to represent God's authority.
options.note: The text names the LORD Himself as Redeemer, not a mediating angelic representative.

quiz.q: What is the LORD's verdict on the idols by the chapter's end, verses 28 to 29?

options.text: They are a delusion, their works amount to nothing, and their images are as empty as the wind.
options.note: Verse 29 delivers exactly this final verdict against the idols.

options.text: They are equally powerful rivals to the LORD.
options.note: The opposite; the entire courtroom scene proves the idols utterly powerless in comparison to the LORD.

options.text: They are useful helpers who share some of the LORD's authority.
options.note: The chapter's verdict is total emptiness, not partial usefulness or shared authority.

options.text: They are dangerous but ultimately unpredictable forces.
options.note: The verdict is not unpredictability but total emptiness, unable to declare or accomplish anything at all.

questions: The nations respond to fear by frantically strengthening their idols. What do you rush to reinforce or lean on when you feel afraid, instead of turning to God?
God calls Israel a worm, yet promises to make that worm able to crush mountains. Where do you feel most weak or insignificant, and how might God want to use exactly that weakness?
The LORD repeats, 'do not fear, I will help you,' several times in this chapter. Which of your current fears do you need to hear this promise applied to most directly?
God is called Israel's Redeemer, a kinsman bound to rescue His own. How does knowing Christ became your kinsman in the flesh change how you receive His help?

The chapter's courtroom exposes idols as empty wind, unable to declare anything true about the future. What modern 'idols', plans, people, or possessions, are you tempted to trust the way ancient Israel was tempted to trust carved images?

translationNotes.note: 'One from the east' most likely anticipates Cyrus of Persia, whose rise is named explicitly in Isaiah 44:28 and 45:1, though the geographic description here remains poetic rather than a precise itinerary.
Worm is a deliberately humbling image in Hebrew, used elsewhere of Israel's lowliness, making the promise of strength that follows all the more striking as entirely God's doing.
'I, the LORD, the first and the last' is a title of eternal self-existence that the risen Christ applies to Himself in Revelation 1:17, a significant point of continuity between the Testaments.
